newsitem.title: USA: Former Treasury counsel arrested in fraud scheme.
newsitem.headline: Former Treasury counsel arrested in fraud scheme.

text.p: A former general counsel to the Treasury Department and three others have been arrested for an alleged scheme to solicit investments in non-existent bank obligations, federal prosecutors said Friday.

Paul Eggers, who had been general counsel to the the Treasury during the Nixon administration, and the other defendants were charged in Manhattan federal court with allegedly collecting nearly $8 million from investors for a program known as "cash leasing."
The other defendants in the scheme are G. Lincecum, Anthony Miremadi and Valerie Miremadi. No details were immediately available from prosecutors about the defendants' residences or employment.
If convicted, the defendants face a possible maxium prison term of 5 years and $1 million in fines.

The complaint alleges that the defendants solicited investors to provide money that Eggers and Lincecum would invest in what were called "106-guarantees," which Lincecum defined as financial instuments issued by "top 25 banks."

He allegedly identified the issuing banks as Bank of Nova Scotia; Barclays Bank, Deutsche Bank, Dressner Bank, Barnett Bank, First Union Bank of Tennessee, ABN Amro Bank and National Westminster Bank.
Lincecum allegedly claimed that he and Eggers had previously obtained such guarantees from the Bank of Nova Scotia and Barclay's Bank, the complaint said.

He also claimed that the guarantees secured the investors' money at a value of 106 percent or 108 percent and were the basis for further investments through what were called "bank guarantee pay-orders" that would yield returns of up to 125 percent.

The profit from the pay order investment was then to be used to purchase "108 guarantees" which in turn were used to "lease" much larger amounts of currency at a fee of 1.55 percent of the total leased amount, the complaint charged.

These terms were stated in a prospectus offered by the defendants. Eggers and Lincecum were listed as the principal investment managers. Lincecum also allegedly claimed the programs were approved the International Monetary Fund.
The prospectus promised an investment return of about $10.4 million for an investment of $500,000 within 60 days.

Prosecutors alleged that many of the defendants' representations were false. They said that the so-called 106- or 108 bank guarantee is not a recognized bank instrument and instead was commonly used in fraud schemes. They said none of the banks referred to by the defendants provide or trade in such guarantees.
